unit.unitOverview: Reported speech has a reputation for being mechanical, and the mechanism is real: tenses shift back, pronouns change, time words move. But the mechanism is the easy half. The harder half is that the verb you choose to report with — said, claimed, admitted, insisted — tells the reader what you think, and choosing it carelessly is how you take a side without noticing. It ends with one statement reported three ways.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. There are four patterns and they build in order.
Open Patterns. Card 2 is the one where word order catches everybody.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is one statement reported three ways.
Do the Practice. Practice 4 is the diagnostic — which verb takes a side.
Record yourself reporting a conversation you actually had.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
Reported speech is what you use every time you tell somebody what somebody else said, which is a large proportion of everything anybody says.
First pattern: reported statements, and the shift.
Direct speech: I am waiting.
Reported: She said she was waiting.
Three things changed and they change together.
The tense went back one step. Am became was.
The pronoun changed. I became she, because the speaker is no longer speaking.
And if there were a time or place word, it would move too, which is card four.
The tense shift is systematic and it is one step back each time.
Present simple goes to past simple. I work becomes she worked.
Present continuous goes to past continuous. I am waiting becomes she was waiting.
Past simple goes to past perfect. I saw it becomes she had seen it.
Present perfect goes to past perfect as well. I have finished becomes she had finished.
Will goes to would. I will come becomes she would come.
Can goes to could. Must goes to had to.
Notice that past simple and present perfect both land on the past perfect, which means some information is lost. She had seen it could have been I saw it or I have seen it. That is a real limitation of the system and there is nothing to be done about it.
And two things that do not shift, because they are already as far back as they go. Past perfect stays past perfect. And would, could, should and might do not shift either.
Now the important exception, and it is not really an exception.
You do not have to shift the tense when the thing is still true.
She said the office closes at six. That is still true, so leaving it in the present is natural.
She said the office closed at six also works, and it very slightly suggests you are only reporting rather than endorsing.
Both are correct. This is not a case with a right answer, and learners spend a lot of time worrying about it unnecessarily.
Second pattern: reported questions, and here there is a real trap.
When you report a question, it stops being a question. So it loses the question word order and it loses the question mark.
Direct: Where do you work?
Reported: She asked where I worked.
Not she asked where did I work. That is the error, and it is extremely common, because the sentence still feels like a question.
The test: after you have written it, does the reported clause read as a statement? Where I worked is a statement. Where did I work is not.
So the helper disappears, exactly as it appeared in Level 1 Unit 16, and the word order goes back to subject then verb.
And for yes/no questions, where there is no question word, you need if or whether.
Direct: Are you ready?
Reported: She asked if I was ready. Or whether I was ready.
If and whether are interchangeable here. Whether is slightly more formal and it is the one to use in writing, particularly when there is an or — she asked whether I wanted tea or coffee.
Third pattern: reported commands and requests.
This one is easier than the others, because it does not use a clause at all. It uses to plus the verb.
Direct: Wait here.
Reported: She told me to wait there.
Direct: Please don't touch that.
Reported: She asked me not to touch it.
Notice the negative: not goes before to. Not to touch, never to not touch.
And notice that these verbs need a person. She told me. She asked me. You cannot say she told to wait.
Fourth pattern: said and told, and the time words.
Said and told are the two commonest reporting verbs and they behave differently.
Told needs a person immediately after it. She told me. She told the manager.
Said does not take a person directly. She said she was waiting. If you want a person with said, you need to: she said to me.
So: she told me, and she said to me. Never she said me, and never she told that.
Then the time and place words, which shift because the moment of speaking has moved.
Now becomes then. Today becomes that day. Tomorrow becomes the next day. Yesterday becomes the day before. Here becomes there. This becomes that. Ago becomes before.
She said, I saw him here yesterday becomes she said she had seen him there the day before.
But — and this matters — you only shift when the shift is needed. If you are reporting on the same day, in the same place, today is still today.
She said she would come today. If it is still today, that is correct and shifting it to that day would be strange.
So the rule is not shift everything. It is: shift what has actually changed.
And the last thing, which is the most important in the unit and is not grammar at all.
The reporting verb you choose carries your judgement.
She said she had checked it. Neutral. You are reporting.
She claimed she had checked it. You are signalling doubt.
She admitted she had checked it. You are implying it was wrong to.
She insisted she had checked it. You are suggesting she was under pressure and would not move.
Same words spoken. Four completely different reports, and the difference is one verb.
That is enormously useful when you mean it, and it is how you take a side without noticing when you do not. In anything that has to be fair — a report, a statement, a summary of somebody else's position — said is the verb that does not editorialise, and it is usually the right choice.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: One Step Back, and When Not To
readings.passageScript:
The mechanism of reported speech is systematic, and it is one step back each time.
Present simple to past simple. I work becomes she worked.
Present continuous to past continuous. I am waiting becomes she was waiting.
Past simple to past perfect. I saw it becomes she had seen it.
Present perfect to past perfect as well. I have finished becomes she had finished.
Will to would, can to could, must to had to.
Two things do not shift because they cannot go further back. Past perfect stays as it is. And would, could, should and might are already shifted forms, so they stay too.
One consequence of the system is worth noticing. Past simple and present perfect both land on the past perfect, which means information is lost. She had seen it might report I saw it or I have seen it, and the reported version cannot tell you which. Nothing can be done about this and it is not your error when it happens.
Now the part learners worry about far more than they need to.
You do not have to shift the tense when what was said is still true.
She said the office closes at six. Still true, so the present is natural.
She said the office closed at six. Also correct, and it very slightly distances you — you are reporting rather than confirming.
Both are right. This is not a case with a single correct answer, and the amount of anxiety it generates is out of proportion to how much it matters.
The same applies to time words. They shift because the moment of speaking has moved — today becomes that day, here becomes there, tomorrow becomes the next day.
But only shift what has actually changed. If you are reporting on the same day, in the same room, today is still today and here is still here.
She said she would come today. If it is still today, that is exactly right, and shifting it to that day would be strange.
The rule is not shift everything. It is shift what has moved.

readings.title: The Verb Is the Judgement
readings.passageScript:
The grammar of reported speech is the easy half. This is the other half, and it matters more.
Somebody says: I checked it on Tuesday.
You can report that four ways, all of them grammatically identical.
She said she had checked it on Tuesday.
She claimed she had checked it on Tuesday.
She admitted she had checked it on Tuesday.
She insisted she had checked it on Tuesday.
Nothing has changed except one verb, and the four reports say very different things.
Said is neutral. You are reporting and nothing more.
Claimed signals doubt. You are telling the reader you do not necessarily believe her, without saying so.
Admitted implies that checking it was somehow wrong, or that she was reluctant to say. It carries a whole story that may not exist.
Insisted suggests she was under pressure and would not move — again, a story.
None of those three is a lie. Each of them is an interpretation smuggled into a verb, and readers absorb it without noticing they have been told what to think.
This is why the choice matters practically.
In journalism, claimed and admitted are used deliberately and are widely criticised for exactly this reason. In an incident report or a summary of somebody's position, the same verbs will make a fair account read as an accusation.
So the working rule is straightforward. When your job is to report fairly — a statement, a summary, minutes, an account of a disagreement — use said. It is the only verb in the group that does not editorialise.
Use the loaded verbs when you actually mean them and when the reader can see your reasoning. She denied it is fair if there was an accusation to deny. She admitted it is fair if there was something to admit.
And watch for them in what you read. When a document reports one side with said and the other with claimed, that document has taken a position, and it has done so in a way that is easy to miss.

readings.title: The Same Words, Three Reports
readings.setting: What a supervisor said at a meeting, and three written accounts of it.
readings.passageScript:
WHAT WAS ACTUALLY SAID

  "I checked the trolley loading on
  Tuesday. It was within the line then.
  I haven't checked it since, because
  I've been on the other bay all week.
  If it's over the line now, that
  happened after Tuesday."

-----------------------------------------

  REPORT A - the incident file

  The supervisor said she had checked the
  trolley loading on the Tuesday and that
  it had been within the marked line at
  that time. She said she had not checked
  it since, as she had been working on
  another bay. She said that any
  overloading had therefore occurred after
  the Tuesday.

-----------------------------------------

  REPORT B - a summary sent upward

  The supervisor claimed she had checked
  the loading on Tuesday and insisted it
  had been within the line. She admitted
  she had not checked it since. She
  maintained that any overloading must
  have happened afterwards.

-----------------------------------------

  REPORT C - a note to the team

  Loading was last checked on Tuesday and
  was within the line. It has not been
  checked since. Anything over the line
  now has happened since Tuesday, so
  please check your own trolleys today.

grammar.title: Reported statements: the shift
grammar.explanation: Tense goes back one step and pronouns change, because the speaker is no longer speaking. The system is regular, and the useful part is knowing when not to apply it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
ONE STEP BACK
  present simple -> past simple
     I work        -> she worked
  present continuous -> past continuous
     I am waiting  -> she was waiting
  past simple -> past perfect
     I saw it      -> she had seen it
  present perfect -> past perfect
     I have finished -> she had finished
  will -> would    can -> could
  must -> had to

PRONOUNS CHANGE TOO
  "I am waiting" -> she said SHE was waiting

WHAT DOES NOT SHIFT
  past perfect - already as far back as
     it goes
  would, could, should, might - already
     shifted forms

INFORMATION IS LOST
  "I saw it" and "I have seen it"
  both -> she had seen it.
  Nothing can be done about that.

DO NOT SHIFT IF IT IS STILL TRUE
  She said the office closes at six.
     ^ still true, present is natural
  She said the office closed at six.
     ^ also fine, slightly more distant
  Both correct. Do not agonise.
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody says: I am waiting for the part.
1. Find the tense. Present continuous.
2. Shift it back one step. Present continuous becomes past continuous: was waiting.
3. Change the pronoun. The speaker is no longer speaking, so I becomes she.
4. Result: She said she was waiting for the part.
Now one that does not shift. Somebody says: the office closes at six.
1. Is it still true? Yes — the office still closes at six.
2. So you may leave it: She said the office closes at six.
3. Or shift it: She said the office closed at six. That is also correct and slightly more distanced.
Neither is wrong. The choice is about whether you are confirming the fact or only reporting that it was said.
And one where information disappears. Somebody says: I have checked it. Reported, that becomes she had checked it — which is what I checked it would also become. The report cannot preserve the difference, and that is a property of English rather than a mistake.
grammar.commonMistake: Shifting mechanically when the fact is still true, producing she said the office closed at six about an office that still closes at six. It is not wrong, but applied to everything it makes ordinary reports sound oddly historical. The other error is forgetting the pronoun: she said I was waiting reports somebody saying that you were waiting, which is a different sentence.
grammar.memoryTip: One step back, and change the pronoun. Leave it alone if it is still true.
grammar.practice:
Report each statement.
1. "I am waiting for the part."
2. "I work in the warehouse."
3. "I saw it on Tuesday."
4. "I have finished."
5. "I will come tomorrow."
6. "The office closes at six." (still true)
grammar.answerKey:
1. She said she was waiting for the part.
2. She said she worked in the warehouse.
3. She said she had seen it on the Tuesday.
4. She said she had finished.
5. She said she would come the next day.
6. She said the office closes at six. (or: closed at six — both fine)
Numbers 3 and 4 both land on the past perfect, from a past simple and a present perfect respectively. That is the information loss the card describes.
Number 6 is the one that has no single right answer, and knowing that saves more time than getting it right does.

grammar.title: Reported questions
grammar.explanation: When a question is reported it stops being a question, so it loses the question word order and the question mark. This is where the commonest error in the unit lives.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
IT IS NO LONGER A QUESTION
  so: statement word order, no ? mark

  "Where do you work?"
  -> She asked where I worked.
  NOT she asked where did I work.

  The helper DISAPPEARS - the reverse of
  Level 1 Unit 16, where it appeared.

WITH A QUESTION WORD
  "When did it arrive?"
  -> He asked when it had arrived.
  "Who told you?"
  -> He asked who had told me.

WITHOUT ONE - use IF or WHETHER
  "Are you ready?"
  -> She asked if I was ready.
  -> She asked whether I was ready.

  interchangeable. WHETHER is slightly
  more formal, and is the one to use
  when there is an OR:
     she asked whether I wanted tea
     or coffee.

THE TEST
  does the reported clause read as a
  STATEMENT?
     "where I worked"      yes
     "where did I work"    no
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody asks: Where do you work?
1. Choose the reporting verb: asked.
2. Keep the question word at the front: where.
3. Now remove the question machinery. Do disappears — it was only there to make a question, and this is no longer one.
4. Put the words in statement order: I worked. Note the tense shifted back as well.
5. Result: She asked where I worked.
6. Apply the test: does where I worked read as a statement? Yes. Confirmed.
Now a yes/no question: Are you ready?
1. There is no question word, so you need one: if or whether.
2. Shift the tense: are becomes was.
3. Statement order: I was ready.
4. Result: She asked if I was ready.
And no question mark on either, because neither sentence is a question — both are statements about a question that was asked.
grammar.commonMistake: Keeping the question word order — she asked where did I work, she asked was I ready. This is by far the commonest error in the unit and it happens because the sentence still feels like a question. It is not: the question is being described, not asked. The other error is a question mark at the end, which follows from the same confusion.
grammar.memoryTip: It is no longer a question. Statement order, no question mark.
grammar.practice:
Report each question.
1. "Where do you work?"
2. "When did it arrive?"
3. "Who told you?"
4. "Are you ready?"
5. "Have you checked it?"
6. "Do you want tea or coffee?"
grammar.answerKey:
1. She asked where I worked.
2. She asked when it had arrived.
3. She asked who had told me.
4. She asked if I was ready.
5. She asked whether I had checked it.
6. She asked whether I wanted tea or coffee.
Numbers 4, 5 and 6 have no question word, so they need if or whether. Number 6 takes whether because of the or.
Number 3 is worth checking. Who told you was already a subject question with no helper in Level 1 Unit 16, so nothing had to be removed — only the tense shifted.
None of the six ends in a question mark. If any of yours does, it is still being written as a question.

grammar.title: Reported commands and requests
grammar.explanation: The easiest of the four, because it does not use a clause at all. It uses to plus the verb, and it needs a person.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
USE TO + VERB. No that-clause.

  "Wait here."
  -> She told me to wait there.

  "Please check it first."
  -> She asked me to check it first.

THE NEGATIVE: NOT goes BEFORE TO
  "Don't touch that."
  -> She asked me not to touch it.
  NOT "to not touch"

THESE VERBS NEED A PERSON
  she told ME, she asked ME,
  she advised US, she ordered THEM

  NOT "she told to wait"

VERBS THAT WORK THIS WAY
  tell, ask, advise, order, instruct,
  urge, warn, remind, forbid, permit

FORBID ALREADY MEANS "ORDER NOT TO"
  She forbade them to discuss it.
  = She ordered them not to discuss it.
  Do not add a second negative.
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody says: Please don't touch that.
1. This is a request, so use ask.
2. Requests need a person: asked me.
3. Now the verb. Commands and requests take to plus the plain verb, not a clause.
4. It is negative, and not goes before to: not to touch.
5. Change the pronoun or determiner if the situation has moved: that becomes it.
6. Result: She asked me not to touch it.
Now a command: Wait here.
1. A command from somebody with authority takes told or ordered.
2. Add the person: told me.
3. To plus the verb: to wait.
4. Here has become there, because you are no longer in that place.
5. Result: She told me to wait there.
Check both against the two rules: is there a person after the verb, and is not before to rather than after it?
grammar.commonMistake: Writing to not touch instead of not to touch. Both sound plausible and only one is standard. The other error is omitting the person — she told to wait is not a sentence, because tell requires somebody to be told. Ask, advise, order, remind and warn behave the same way.
grammar.memoryTip: To plus the verb, a person after the reporting verb, and not before to.
grammar.practice:
Report each command or request.
1. "Wait here."
2. "Please check it first."
3. "Don't touch that."
4. "Don't sign anything yet."
5. "Report it in writing."
6. "Please don't discuss this outside the team."
grammar.answerKey:
1. She told me to wait there.
2. She asked me to check it first.
3. She asked me not to touch it.
4. He advised me not to sign anything yet.
5. We were instructed to report it in writing.
6. She asked us not to discuss it outside the team.
Every negative has not before to. If you wrote to not touch or to not sign, that is the one error this card exists to prevent.
Every one names a person — me, us, or the passive we were, which contains the person as the subject.
Number 1 changed here to there, because the reporting is happening somewhere else.

grammar.title: Said, told, time words, and the verb that judges
grammar.explanation: Three small things and one large one. The large one is that your reporting verb tells the reader what you think, and choosing it carelessly takes a side.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
SAID vs TOLD
  TOLD needs a person straight after it
     she told me / she told the manager
  SAID does not take a person directly
     she said she was waiting
     she said TO me

  NOT "she said me"
  NOT "she told that"

TIME AND PLACE WORDS SHIFT
  now -> then          here -> there
  today -> that day    this -> that
  tomorrow -> the next day
  yesterday -> the day before
  ago -> before

  BUT only shift what has MOVED.
  Same day, same room? today is today.

THE VERB CARRIES YOUR JUDGEMENT
  She SAID she had checked it.
     neutral. Just reporting.
  She CLAIMED she had checked it.
     you signal doubt.
  She ADMITTED she had checked it.
     you imply it was wrong to.
  She INSISTED she had checked it.
     you suggest pressure and refusal.

  Same words spoken. Four reports.

  When the job is to report FAIRLY,
  use SAID. It is the only one that
  does not editorialise.
grammar.workedExample:
A supervisor says, on Tuesday: I checked it today and it was fine.
You are writing the incident file on Thursday.
1. Choose the verb. This is a factual record that has to be fair, so said.
2. Shift the tense: checked becomes had checked, was becomes had been.
3. Shift the time word — you are reporting two days later, so today has moved: that day, or on the Tuesday.
4. Result: She said she had checked it on the Tuesday and that it had been fine.
Now the same words, reported carelessly: She claimed she had checked it and insisted it had been fine.
Nothing untrue has been written. But claimed tells the reader you doubt her, and insisted suggests she was resisting pressure that may never have existed. The file now contains an accusation nobody made.
And a time word that should not shift. If you were writing the file on the same Tuesday, she said she had checked it today would be correct — today has not moved, so nor should the word.
grammar.commonMistake: Using claimed, admitted or insisted in a document that is meant to be neutral. Each is defensible sentence by sentence and the accumulation takes a side. The other errors are mechanical: she said me and she told that, and shifting time words that have not moved — writing that day about something happening today.
grammar.memoryTip: Told takes a person, said does not. Shift what has moved. Use said when it must be fair.
grammar.practice:
Correct or complete each one.
1. She ____ me she was waiting. (said or told)
2. She ____ she was waiting. (said or told)
3. She ____ to me that it was ready. (said or told)
4. "I saw him here yesterday." — report it a week later.
5. "I will come today." — report it the same day.
6. Report "I checked it" three ways: neutrally, with doubt, and implying reluctance.
grammar.answerKey:
1. told — it has a person immediately after it.
2. said — no person follows.
3. said — said takes to before a person.
4. She said she had seen him there the day before.
5. She said she would come today. — today has not moved, so it stays.
6. She said she had checked it. / She claimed she had checked it. / She admitted she had checked it.
Numbers 4 and 5 are the pair that matters. In 4 the report happens a week later, so here and yesterday both shift. In 5 it happens the same day, so today stays — shifting it to that day would be wrong.
In number 6, only the first is fair reporting. The other two are interpretations, and both would be out of place in a record that has to be checkable later.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A conversation reported
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write out a conversation you have had, real or invented, as direct speech — at least twelve lines with speech marks.
Then report the whole thing.
Use at least six reported statements, three reported questions and three reported commands or requests.
Use said and told correctly at least twice each.

writing.modelText:
DIRECT:
"Have you checked the loading on bay two?"
"I checked it on Tuesday. It was within the line then."
"Why haven't you checked it since?"
"I've been on the other bay all week."
"Who's been covering bay two?"
"Nobody, as far as I know."
"Please check it before you leave today."
"I can't — I finish at two and the delivery isn't in until four."
"Then don't let anyone load it until it's been checked."
"I'll put a note on it."
"And tell me tomorrow what you find."
"I will."

REPORTED:
He asked her whether she had checked the loading on bay two. She said she had checked it on the Tuesday and that it had been within the line then. He asked why she had not checked it since, and she said she had been working on the other bay all week. He asked who had been covering bay two and she said nobody had, as far as she knew.
He asked her to check it before she left that day. She said she could not, because she finished at two and the delivery was not due until four. He told her not to let anyone load it until it had been checked, and she said she would put a note on it. He asked her to tell him the next day what she found, and she said she would.

Not shifted: none — this report is written a week later, so today became that day and tomorrow became the next day throughout.

writing.title: Writing 2 — One statement, three reports
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Take one statement — from Reading 3, from a conversation you had, or invented.
Write three reports of it, as in Reading 3.
Report A: neutral and fully attributed, using said throughout.
Report B: the same content with loaded reporting verbs — claimed, admitted, insisted, maintained.

writing.modelText:
Original: "I sent the file on Thursday. I didn't get a reply, so I assumed it had gone through. I've only just found out it bounced."

A. She said she had sent the file on the Thursday. She said she had not received a reply and had therefore assumed it had gone through. She said she had only just discovered that it had bounced.

B. She claimed she had sent the file on the Thursday. She admitted she had not received a reply but insisted she had assumed it had gone through. She maintained that she had only just discovered it had bounced.

C. The file was sent on Thursday. No reply was received. The bounce was discovered late. Please check delivery confirmations in future.

1. B implies she is not believed about sending it, that failing to notice the lack of reply was a fault she had to concede, and that she is defending herself under pressure. None of that is in what she said.
2. C loses the source completely. Nobody reading it knows this is one person's account rather than a verified finding, and the passive removes her from her own actions — the file was sent, by nobody.
3. A, for any record that might be checked later. It attributes everything, uses a neutral verb, and keeps the difference between what she did and what she assumed.
writing.successCriteria: All three reports contain the same content; A uses said throughout and attributes everything; B changes only the verbs; C removes attribution entirely; three lines identifying B's implications, C's loss, and a justified preference
writing.support: Write A first and then change nothing but the verbs to make B. If you find yourself changing anything else, B is doing more than the exercise asks and the comparison stops being clean.
writing.extension: Show B to somebody without showing them the original, and ask what they think of the speaker. Then show them the original.

2. That she is not believed, that she was under pressure and resisting it, and that not having checked since was something to be extracted from her. The original contains none of that — she volunteered it as an explanation.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the twelve
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. She said she is waiting. (she said it last week and is no longer waiting)
2. She said I was waiting. (you mean she was waiting)
3. She asked where did I work.
4. He asked when had it arrived.
5. She asked was I ready.
6. She asked me where I worked?
7. She told me not to not touch it.
8. She asked me to not sign anything.
9. She told to wait there.
10. She said me she would come.
11. She said she would come that day. (you are reporting it today, and she means today)

1. She said she was waiting. (Pattern 1 — the tense shifts back when the situation has changed)
2. She said she was waiting. (Pattern 1 — the pronoun must change to she)
3. She asked where I worked. (Pattern 2 — a reported question takes statement word order)
4. He asked when it had arrived. (Pattern 2 — same rule)
5. She asked if I was ready. (Pattern 2 — no question word, so if or whether)
6. She asked me where I worked. (Pattern 2 — it is no longer a question, so no question mark)
7. She told me not to touch it. (Pattern 3 — one negative, and not goes before to)
8. She asked me not to sign anything. (Pattern 3 — not before to, never to not)
9. She told me to wait there. (Pattern 3 — tell needs a person)
10. She told me she would come. (Pattern 4 — said does not take a person directly; told does)
11. She said she would come today. (Pattern 4 — shift only what has moved)
12. She said she had checked it. (Pattern 4 — a neutral record takes said)

activities.title: Practice 1 — Report the statement
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Report each one, shifting tense and pronouns.
1. "I am waiting for the part."
2. "I work in the warehouse."
3. "I saw it on Tuesday."
4. "I have finished."
5. "I will come tomorrow."
6. "I can do it on Friday."
7. "I must leave at four."
8. "I had already checked it."
9. "I might be late."
10. "I don't know."
11. "The office closes at six." (still true)
12. "I've been trying to reach you all week."
activities.answerSummary:
1. She said she was waiting for the part.
2. She said she worked in the warehouse.
3. She said she had seen it on the Tuesday.
4. She said she had finished.
5. She said she would come the next day.
6. She said she could do it on the Friday.
7. She said she had to leave at four.
8. She said she had already checked it. — no shift; past perfect cannot go further back.
9. She said she might be late. — no shift; might is already a shifted form.
10. She said she did not know.
11. She said the office closes at six. (or closed — both correct)
12. She said she had been trying to reach me all week.
Numbers 8 and 9 do not shift, and the card explains why: both are already as far back as English goes.
Numbers 3 and 4 both land on the past perfect from different starting points, which is where the information loss happens.
Number 12 shifts a present perfect continuous to a past perfect continuous, and the pronoun changed from you to me because the reporter is the person who was being contacted.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Report the question
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Report each question. No question marks.
1. "Where do you work?"
2. "When did it arrive?"
3. "Who told you?"
4. "Are you ready?"
5. "Have you checked it?"
6. "Do you want tea or coffee?"
7. "Why didn't you tell me?"
8. "What happened?"
9. "Can you come on Friday?"
10. "How long will it take?"
11. "Did anybody see it?"
12. "Whose responsibility is it?"
activities.answerSummary:
1. She asked where I worked.
2. She asked when it had arrived.
3. She asked who had told me.
4. She asked if I was ready.
5. She asked whether I had checked it.
6. She asked whether I wanted tea or coffee.
7. She asked why I had not told her.
8. She asked what had happened.
9. She asked if I could come on the Friday.
10. She asked how long it would take.
11. She asked whether anybody had seen it.
12. She asked whose responsibility it was.
Four of the twelve — 4, 5, 6, 9 and 11 — have no question word and need if or whether. Number 6 takes whether because of the or.
Numbers 3 and 8 were already subject questions with no helper, so only the tense shifted. Everything else lost a do, did or an inversion.
None ends in a question mark. Every reported clause reads as a statement, which is the test.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Report the command
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Report each command or request, using to plus the verb.
1. "Wait here."
2. "Please check it first."
3. "Don't touch that."
4. "Don't sign anything yet."
5. "Report it in writing."
6. "Please don't discuss this outside the team."
7. "Come back tomorrow."
8. "Don't use the lift."
9. "Get it in writing."
10. "Please don't move the trolley."
11. "Tell me if anything changes."
12. "Don't wait for me."
activities.answerSummary:
1. She told me to wait there.
2. She asked me to check it first.
3. She told me not to touch it.
4. He advised me not to sign anything yet.
5. We were instructed to report it in writing.
6. She asked us not to discuss it outside the team.
7. He told me to come back the next day.
8. The notice told us not to use the lift.
9. She advised me to get it in writing.
10. She asked us not to move the trolley.
11. She asked me to tell her if anything changed.
12. He told me not to wait for him.
Six are negative — 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12 — and every one has not before to. If any of yours reads to not, that is the error.
Every one names a person. Where the original had no addressee, the report supplies one: we were instructed, the notice told us.
Numbers 1 and 7 shifted here and tomorrow, because the report is happening elsewhere and later.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Which verb takes a side?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write NEUTRAL or LOADED. For each loaded one, say what it implies about the reporter's view.
1. She said she had checked it.
2. She claimed she had checked it.
3. She admitted she had checked it.
4. She insisted she had checked it.
5. She stated that no fault was found.
6. She denied that she had been told.
7. She mentioned that the deadline had moved.
8. She boasted that she had finished in a day.
9. She noted that the figures did not match.
10. She complained that nobody had told her.
11. She reported that two machines had failed.
12. She confessed that she had not read it.
13. She added that the cost had not been agreed.
14. She maintained that there was no fault.
15. She observed that nobody had asked the night shift.
16. She reassured us that the deadline had not moved.
activities.answerSummary:
NEUTRAL: 1, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15.
LOADED: 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16.
2. claimed — signals you doubt her.
3. admitted — implies checking it was wrong, or that she was reluctant.
4. insisted — suggests pressure and refusal to move.
6. denied — presupposes an accusation was made.
8. boasted — strongly negative about the speaker.
10. complained — frames her as dissatisfied rather than informative.
12. confessed — much stronger than admitted; implies shame.
14. maintained — suggests she is holding a position under challenge.
16. reassured — positive, but it implies the listeners were worried and that she was right to calm them.
Number 16 is the one people miss. Loaded does not mean negative — reassured takes a side in the speaker's favour, and in a neutral record that is just as much an intrusion.
Numbers 6 and 14 are fair when there really was an accusation or a challenge. Loaded verbs are not forbidden; they are claims, and they should be true.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Report something you were told
activities.instructionsAndItems:
This week, report one real conversation to somebody in writing — a message summarising what was said, or notes from a discussion.
Use said throughout, even where a stronger verb is tempting.
Mark every point where you wanted a loaded verb.
Then write one line for each mark, saying what you would have implied and whether you could have justified it.
activities.answerSummary:
No key — it is your conversation.
What most people find: two or three points where a loaded verb was tempting, and they cluster around the same thing — a moment where the other person said something the writer did not believe, or explained something the writer thought was an excuse.
That is exactly where claimed appears in real documents, and it is exactly where it is least defensible, because at that point the writer has a view and the verb smuggles it in.
The second finding is that the neutral version is usually shorter, because said needs no justification and claimed invites the reader to ask why.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Count the verbs in the news
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Find one news report that quotes two or more people or organisations.
Write down every reporting verb it uses and who each one is attached to.
Then check whether the verbs are distributed evenly, or whether one side gets said and another gets claimed, denied or insisted.
Write one line on what the distribution suggests.
activities.answerSummary:
No key.
What most people find: the distribution is rarely even, and the asymmetry is the finding. When one party is consistently reported with said and another with claimed or insisted, the report has taken a position without ever stating one.
The second finding is about denied. It appears constantly and it is the most quietly loaded verb in the set, because it presupposes an accusation. Reporting somebody as denying something tells the reader there was a charge to answer, even where the sentence never says what it was.
The third finding, which is worth holding on to: this is not usually deliberate deception. Journalists write at speed and reach for variation, because repeating said looks repetitive. Repeating said is nevertheless the fair choice, and the pressure not to is what makes the pattern so common.

teacherNotes.note: The tense and pronoun shifts are systematic and most learners get them within a session. The verb-choice half is where the unit's value is, and it is almost never taught. teacherNotes.noteType: Reported questions are the persistent error
teacherNotes.note: She asked where did I work survives long after the rule is understood, because the sentence still feels like a question. The fix is the test — read the reported clause alone and ask whether it is a statement — and it needs drilling in speech rather than writing. teacherNotes.note: Learners taught a full time-word table apply it mechanically and produce that day about something happening today. Reading 1 and card 4 both state the rule as shift what has moved, and Practice 4 number 5 and Writing 4 number 11 test the non-shift specifically. What most people find: two or three points where a loaded verb was tempting, and they cluster around the same thing — a moment where the other person said something the writer did not believe, or explained something the writer thought was an excuse.
That is exactly where claimed appears in real documents, and it is exactly where it is least defensible, because at that point the writer has a view and the verb smuggles it in.
The second finding is that the neutral version is usually shorter, because said needs no justification and claimed invites the reader to ask why.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
No key.
What most people find: the distribution is rarely even, and the asymmetry is the finding. When one party is consistently reported with said and another with claimed or insisted, the report has taken a position without ever stating one.
The second finding is about denied. It appears constantly and it is the most quietly loaded verb in the set, because it presupposes an accusation. Reporting somebody as denying something tells the reader there was a charge to answer, even where the sentence never says what it was.
The third finding, which is worth holding on to: this is not usually deliberate deception. Journalists write at speed and reach for variation, because repeating said looks repetitive. Repeating said is nevertheless the fair choice, and the pressure not to is what makes the pattern so common.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She said she was waiting. — The tense goes back one step and the pronoun changes, because the speaker is no longer speaking. Both changes happen together.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: past perfect — It is already as far back as English goes. Would, could, should and might do not shift either, for the same reason.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Yes — you need not shift a fact that is still true — Closed would also be correct and slightly more distanced. This is a case with no single right answer, which is worth knowing because it saves a lot of unnecessary worry.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She asked where I worked. — A reported question is no longer a question, so it takes statement word order, the helper disappears, and there is no question mark.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She asked if I was ready. — With no question word you need if or whether. Whether is slightly more formal and is required when there is an or.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She told me not to touch it. — Not goes before to, and tell requires a person. To not touch sounds plausible and is not the standard form.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She told me she would come. — Told takes a person immediately after it; said does not. If you want a person with said, you need to — she said to me.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: It stays today — Shift only what has actually moved. Applying the shift table mechanically produces that day about something happening today, which reads oddly.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: That the reporter doubts her — Nothing untrue has been written, and the doubt is smuggled into the verb. Readers absorb it without noticing they have been told what to think.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: said — It is the only one in the group that does not editorialise. The others are all interpretations, and each is defensible sentence by sentence while the accumulation takes a side.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Only in the reporting verbs — The content, the tense shifts and the order are identical. Four verbs are the entire difference, and they change what the reader concludes about the speaker.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The source — Nobody reading it knows the information came from one person's account rather than a verified check, so nobody can go back and weigh it.
